name: Master of Research in Cyber, Policing, Intelligence, Counter Terrorism, Security Studies and Criminology
description:
This is a research degree, not a coursework master's, and that distinction matters more here than in most program listings: Macquarie's Master of Research (MRes) is explicitly built as a training pathway toward a PhD or Master of Philosophy rather than a standalone professional qualification, and this particular award lets students specialise their research within the Department of Security Studies and Criminology across cyber security, policing, intelligence, counter terrorism, security studies or criminology. Anyone weighing this against Macquarie's separate coursework Master of Cyber-Security, Policing, Intelligence and Counter Terrorism should understand these are genuinely different degrees serving different purposes, one trains researchers, the other trains practitioners.

The structure runs in two parts across two years full-time: a Graduate Diploma year (Part A) of intensive coursework building research skills specific to the discipline, followed by a second year (Part B) spent producing a roughly 20,000-word thesis on a self-defined research problem within the security, policing or criminology space. Admission to progress from MRes to a doctorate depends directly on the final MRes mark: a mark of 65-74% typically supports progression to an MPhil, while 75% and above supports progression to a full PhD, so the second-year thesis grade functions as a genuine gatekeeping mechanism rather than a formality.

Given Macquarie's Department of Security Studies and Criminology sits within a policy-facing research environment with strong Canberra and law-enforcement links, students often use the MRes thesis to build a body of original research on an Australian security or policing problem that then carries directly into a funded PhD project, rather than starting a doctorate from a blank slate.
curriculum:
Part A (Year 1, Graduate Diploma level): research methods and design, discipline-specific advanced seminars in security studies, criminology, policing or counter terrorism, literature review and research proposal development
Part B (Year 2): supervised original research culminating in an approximately 20,000-word thesis
Specialisation areas: Cyber Security, Policing, Intelligence, Counter Terrorism, Security Studies, Criminology (student selects a research focus within the department)
Progression outcomes: final mark 65-74% supports progression to Master of Philosophy (MPhil); 75%+ supports progression to PhD
Structure: 2 years full-time (or 4 years part-time)
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree with honours or equivalent research background

name: Master of Translation and Interpreting Studies
description:
Macquarie's translation and interpreting program is approved by NAATI, Australia's national accrediting body for translators and interpreters, at professional level, which is the credential that actually lets graduates work as certified translators or interpreters in Australia rather than simply having studied the field academically. Students choose a language pair with English from Chinese (Mandarin), French, Japanese, Korean or Spanish, and the coursework runs alongside a separate, more specialised Master of Conference Interpreting for students aiming specifically at simultaneous interpreting careers rather than the broader translation and interpreting scope covered here.

Because NAATI accreditation is assessed against specific competency standards rather than general coursework completion, the degree is built around practical translation and interpreting exercises, legal and medical interpreting scenarios, ethics and professional conduct, alongside the linguistic theory underpinning translation practice, rather than treating professional accreditation as a separate add-on qualification students pursue after finishing an academic degree.

Sydney's demographic mix, with large first-generation communities across the five language pairs on offer, means placement and practicum opportunities for students in this program are unusually concrete: court interpreting, community health interpreting and settlement services all draw on graduates of programs exactly like this one, which is a different career pipeline from the conference and diplomatic interpreting track that the separate Master of Conference Interpreting targets.
curriculum:
Core units: translation theory and practice, interpreting theory and practice, professional ethics and conduct for translators/interpreters, consecutive and simultaneous interpreting techniques
Applied practicum units: legal interpreting, medical/health interpreting, community and liaison interpreting, specialised translation (legal, technical, business texts)
Language pairs available: Chinese (Mandarin), French, Japanese, Korean, Spanish (paired with English)
Accreditation: NAATI professional-level approval, subject to satisfying program requirements
Structure: typically 1.5 years full-time (18 months)
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree or equivalent, proficiency in a second language

name: Bachelor of Business
description:
MIT structures its Bachelor of Business so students spend the first year on a broad common core before locking in a major (Contemporary Management, Business Analytics, Marketing and Digital Communications, or Accounting), which gives students who arrive unsure of specialisation a genuine runway to figure it out rather than committing on day one. The Accounting major specifically feeds into professional body accreditation pathways (CPA Australia, CAANZ), which matters for international students planning to stay in Australia and pursue accounting as a migration occupation.

As with MIT's other degrees, the pitch here isn't research prestige. It's practical, industry-connected teaching delivered in smaller classes than a large public university, with a flipped-classroom format and the InSPIRE academic support scheme built specifically around a cohort that skews heavily international. The Business Analytics major overlaps meaningfully with MIT's dedicated Bachelor of Data Analytics, so prospective students choosing between the two need to look closely at how much of each degree is data/technical versus general business content.

MIT runs three intakes a year and offers the degree from both its Melbourne and Sydney campuses, which is a point of flexibility not available at most Australian universities tied to a single February/July semester cycle.
curriculum:
Year 1 (common core): Principles of Management, Marketing Fundamentals, Accounting for Business, Business Economics, Business Law, Business Statistics
Majors (choose one, Years 2-3): Contemporary Management, Business Analytics, Marketing and Digital Communications, Accounting
Capstone: industry-based project or internship in final year
Total: 3 years full-time, 360 credit points, on campus (Melbourne or Sydney), 3 intakes per year
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; foundation/diploma pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Data Analytics
description:
MIT's Bachelor of Data Analytics is built around what the university calls a flipped classroom model: students work through material before class so contact time can go toward applied, hands-on problem-solving rather than lecture delivery, combined with the InSPIRE academic support program aimed at helping students, many of them international, adjust to Australian tertiary assessment expectations. The degree covers the full data analytics lifecycle from data collection through to AI and machine learning applications, rather than treating machine learning as an advanced elective bolted onto a traditional stats degree.

The standout structural feature is the final year, where students complete two separate industry-based capstone projects rather than one, each running through the full systems development lifecycle (specification, analysis, design, development, implementation, testing, troubleshooting) with real industry supervisors involved alongside academic staff. That's a heavier applied-project load than a lot of comparable data analytics undergraduate degrees carry, and it's consistent with MIT's institutional identity as a work-integrated-learning-first provider rather than a research-intensive university.

As a private provider without the research profile of a larger public university, MIT's practical positioning here works well for students who want a direct, applied path into data analyst roles without a heavy theoretical statistics or computer science load.
curriculum:
Core units: Data Science Fundamentals, Programming for Data Analytics, Database Systems, Statistical Methods, Machine Learning Fundamentals, Data Visualisation, Big Data Technologies, Ethics and Governance in Data
Capstone: two industry-based projects in final year, each covering the full analytics/systems development lifecycle
Total: 3 years full-time, on campus (Melbourne or Sydney)
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; foundation/diploma pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Engineering Technology (Telecommunications)
description:
This is the undergraduate, engineering-technologist-level counterpart to MIT's Master of Engineering (Telecommunications): a slightly more applied, hands-on qualification pitched at students who want to work directly with telecommunications infrastructure rather than pursue the more theory-heavy professional engineer accreditation track. The degree runs 24 units totalling 360 credit points, with each standard unit worth 15 credit points, and covers planning, design, implementation and maintenance of telecommunication systems using current hardware and software rather than legacy equipment.

One core unit specifically worth noting is applied mobile and satellite communication systems, covering antennas, microwaves, GPS, and spectrum analysis. That's specialised content that doesn't show up in a generic electrical or IT degree and reflects genuine subject-matter depth in a fairly narrow technical niche. A twelve-week full-time (or 24-week part-time) industry placement is mandatory rather than optional, consistent with MIT's institution-wide emphasis on work-integrated learning, and gives graduates direct workplace telecommunications experience before they finish the degree.

The program is TEQSA-accredited (Australia's higher education regulator), and electives in IT, security, and information systems let students round out the core telecommunications content with adjacent technical skills that broaden employability beyond a single carrier-network-engineer career track.
curriculum:
Core units (24 total, 15 credit points each): Telecommunications Fundamentals, Network Design and Infrastructure, Wireless and Broadband Networks, Applied Mobile and Satellite Communication Systems, Signal Processing, Telecommunications Regulation and Standards, plus IT/security/information systems electives
Work-integrated learning: mandatory 12-week full-time (or 24-week part-time) industry placement
Total: 360 credit points, standard full-time load 60 credit points per trimester (approx. 3 years full-time), TEQSA-accredited, on campus
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion with mathematics; foundation/diploma pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Networking
description:
MIT's Bachelor of Networking is explicitly built around vendor certification alongside the academic degree: coursework maps toward Microsoft Server Administration and Cisco certifications including CCNA, CCNA Wireless, and CCNA Security, which gives graduates a combination of an ACS-accredited (Professional Level) academic qualification and industry-recognised certifications that carry weight independently with employers. That dual-track approach is a meaningful point of difference from a generic IT or computer science degree with a couple of networking electives tacked on.

The course structure moves from common core IT units (programming, information systems, database technology, project management) into networking specialisation electives covering wireless network security, advanced internetworking design, and enterprise cybersecurity, with a dedicated Cyber Security major offered as a named specialisation for students who want to lean that direction specifically. Business electives round out the technical core, and industry-based projects apply the work-integrated learning model MIT uses across its degrees.

Offered from both the Melbourne and Sydney campuses, the degree suits students targeting network engineer, systems administrator, or network security roles who want vendor-recognised certifications as a tangible credential alongside the degree itself, rather than relying purely on the university qualification to signal competency to employers.
curriculum:
Common core: Programming Fundamentals, Information Systems, Database Technology, Software Engineering Principles, IT Project Management
Networking specialisation electives: Wireless Network Security, Advanced Internetworking Design, Enterprise Cybersecurity
Optional major: Cyber Security
Certification alignment: coursework maps to Microsoft Server Administration and Cisco CCNA, CCNA Wireless, CCNA Security
Capstone: industry-based networking project
Total: 3 years full-time, ACS-accredited (Professional Level), on campus (Melbourne or Sydney)
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; foundation/diploma pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Master of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
Master of Business Analytics
description:
This degree is aimed at people who studied something unrelated to data or business as undergraduates and want a fast, structured route into business intelligence and analytics roles: entry only requires an Australian bachelor's degree (or equivalent) in any discipline, not a quantitative or business background specifically. That accessibility is deliberate: it widens the applicant pool to career-changers and international graduates who need a postgraduate qualification aligned to in-demand analytics occupations for Australian skilled migration purposes.

The curriculum sits at the intersection most business analytics programs claim to occupy but don't always deliver on: genuinely teaching both the technical side (gathering, cleaning, and preparing data) and the communication side (presenting findings to non-technical stakeholders), rather than being a rebadged data science or statistics degree with a business label stapled on. MIT built the course in consultation with industry specifically to address a stated skills gap in business intelligence analysts, and the applied, real-world-problem orientation runs through most units rather than being confined to a single capstone.

Given MIT's overall institutional profile, this program is a solid, practically-focused option for someone wanting analytics skills and an Australian postgraduate credential, but it's not positioned to compete with the research depth or industry brand recognition of an analytics degree from a larger research university.
curriculum:
Core units: Data Science Fundamentals, Business Intelligence and Visualisation, Statistical Analysis for Business, Database and Data Warehousing, Predictive Analytics, Ethics in Data and AI, Business Analytics Strategy
Applied component: industry-based analytics project addressing a real organisational problem
Total: 2 years full-time (accelerated options available for eligible applicants), on campus (Melbourne or Sydney)
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree in a related discipline
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Master of Business Research
description:
This is MIT's research-track postgraduate business degree, aimed squarely at students who want either a genuine research career or a stepping stone into a PhD, rather than a coursework MBA-style qualification. The structure runs across two years: the first exposes students to current developments and debates in their chosen business subfield so they can settle on a specific research question, and the second is largely given over to producing a thesis of 20,000 to 30,000 words, with research work beginning toward the end of year one and continuing intensively through year two.

That thesis length sits in a fairly typical range for an Australian research master's, positioned as a genuine scholarly output rather than an extended essay, and it demands a level of independent, self-directed work quite different from MIT's more heavily industry-project-oriented coursework degrees like the Master of Business Analytics or Master of IT. Students considering this route should go in aware it's a smaller, more specialised program than MIT's flagship coursework offerings, better suited to someone with a clear research question already in mind or a genuine interest in academia than someone chasing a general business qualification.

Graduates are positioned either to move directly into industry research roles or to apply for a PhD program, using the thesis as demonstrated evidence of independent research capability.
curriculum:
Year 1: research training coursework, literature review and methodology development, supervised identification of a research topic within business
Year 2: independent thesis research and writing (20,000-30,000 words), regular supervision meetings, final thesis submission and examination
Total: 2 years full-time, research pathway toward industry research roles or PhD candidacy
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree with honours or equivalent research background
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Master of Engineering (Telecommunications)
description:
Telecommunications engineering is one of MIT's more specialised offerings, and it fills a fairly narrow niche in the Australian postgraduate engineering market: few providers run a dedicated telecommunications-focused master's outside broader electrical/electronic engineering programs. The course covers broadband systems, satellite communications, and radio frequency engineering as named subject areas, alongside broader electives in IT, computer networking, and security that round graduates out for roles beyond pure RF or satellite specialism.

Structurally it's 10 core units plus 2 electives, with electives split across level-500 and level-600 (more advanced) study, and a mandatory industry internship built into the program rather than offered as an optional add-on, reflecting MIT's broader institutional emphasis on work-integrated learning as its distinguishing feature relative to larger, more research-oriented engineering schools. Problem-based and project-based learning threads through the degree, aiming to build professional skills like technical communication and project management alongside pure engineering content.

Graduates typically target roles in telecommunications carriers, network infrastructure providers, and increasingly satellite/space communications companies, an area of growing activity in Australia given recent expansion in satellite broadband and low-earth-orbit communications infrastructure.
curriculum:
Core units (10): Broadband Communication Systems, Satellite Communications, Radio Frequency Engineering, Network Design and Architecture, Wireless and Mobile Communications, Telecommunications Project Management, and further core telecommunications units
Electives (2): chosen from IT, computer networking, systems analysis, or security streams (mix of level-500 and level-600 study)
Work-integrated learning: mandatory industry internship
Total: full-time load of 60 credit points per trimester; typically 2 years full-time, on campus
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree in engineering or related discipline
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Master of Information Technology
description:
MIT is a private Melbourne-founded provider (now also running a Sydney campus) that leans heavily on work-integrated learning as its actual point of difference against the bigger public universities it competes with for the same international IT student market. The Master of IT follows that model: coursework builds through programming, information systems, database technology and software engineering, then closes with an industry-based capstone project supervised jointly by academic staff and an external industry partner, rather than a purely academic thesis or exam-based finish.

Classes run on a flipped-classroom model (students work through content before class and use contact time for applied problem-solving), paired with an internal academic support structure called InSPIRE aimed at students who need extra help adjusting, which matters given a large share of MIT's cohort is international students transitioning into an unfamiliar assessment style. Three intakes a year (March, July, November) give more flexible entry timing than the standard two-semester cycle at most Australian universities.

Because MIT doesn't carry the research reputation or brand recognition of a Group of Eight university, the degree's real selling points are practical: smaller class sizes, direct industry project placements, and a faster on-ramp for career changers from non-IT bachelor's backgrounds who need a recognised postgraduate IT qualification for skilled migration purposes.
curriculum:
Core units: Programming Fundamentals, Systems Analysis and Design, Database Technology, Software Engineering, Enterprise Networks, IT Project Management, Cyber Security Principles
Electives: choose from data analytics, advanced networking, or software development streams
Capstone: two industry-based projects in final year, supervised by academic and industry partners
Total: 2 years full-time, on campus (Melbourne or Sydney), 3 intakes per year (March/July/November)
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree (any discipline) typically required (approximate, typical bar, not program-page-verified)
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 overall (typical bar for postgrad at private AU providers, approximate)

name: Master of Networking
description:
The Master of Networking builds on MIT's undergraduate networking offering with two named specialisations, Cyber Security and Cloud Networking, reflecting where enterprise networking demand has shifted over the past several years, away from pure on-premises infrastructure administration and toward cloud-integrated, security-conscious network design. Hands-on practical work with Cisco, Microsoft, and Riverbed networking technology is built into the course rather than kept purely theoretical, which matters for a discipline where employers generally want to see vendor-platform familiarity alongside conceptual knowledge.

Structurally each unit carries 20 credit points with a standard full-time load of 60 credit points per trimester, and the program can be completed in one to two years depending on entry pathway and prior qualifications. MIT offers a shortened pathway for students entering with relevant undergraduate networking or IT credentials. As with MIT's other postgraduate IT and engineering programs, the emphasis throughout is on applied, industry-collaborative learning over pure theory.

Given how quickly cloud networking architectures and security threats evolve, a program like this leans heavily on currency of teaching content and vendor partnerships rather than settled textbook material, so prospective students should look closely at how recently MIT has updated its cloud and security curriculum before enrolling.
curriculum:
Core units: Network Management and System Administration, Network Security Fundamentals, Cloud Infrastructure and Services, Enterprise Network Design, Systems Analysis for Networking Professionals
Specialisations (choose one): Cyber Security, Cloud Networking
Practical component: hands-on labs using Cisco, Microsoft, and Riverbed technology
Total: 1-2 years full-time depending on entry pathway and prior qualifications, on campus (Melbourne or Sydney)
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree in IT or related discipline
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Master of Professional Accounting
description:
The Master of Professional Accounting at MIT is a conversion degree aimed at graduates from any undergraduate discipline who want a recognised accounting qualification, and its accreditation stack is the main reason to choose it over a less formally recognised alternative: CPA Australia, Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand (CA ANZ), and the Institute of Public Accountants (IPA) all accredit the program, which opens direct membership pathways into each body after graduation.

Beyond the accounting fundamentals expected of any professional accounting master's (auditing, taxation, corporate law, financial reporting), the course specifically flags forensic accounting and regulatory compliance as areas of curriculum emphasis, which reflects a broader shift in Australian accounting education toward governance and fraud-detection skills following a string of high-profile corporate compliance failures in the 2010s and 2020s. Employability skills (communication, collaboration, problem-solving, self-direction, leadership) are built into course design as explicit learning outcomes rather than left as incidental byproducts of technical coursework.

Given MIT's institutional profile as a practically oriented private provider, this degree functions well as an efficient professional accreditation pathway for career-changers, though students should weigh it against equivalent CPA/CAANZ-accredited masters at larger universities if brand recognition with graduate employers is a priority.
curriculum:
Core units: Financial Accounting, Management Accounting, Auditing and Assurance, Taxation Law, Corporate Law, Accounting Theory, Forensic Accounting, Economics for Accountants, Accounting Information Systems
Employability skills integration: communication, collaboration, and leadership development embedded across units
Capstone: applied accounting case study or industry project
Accreditation: meets educational requirements for CPA Australia, CA ANZ, and IPA membership
Total: 2 years full-time (shorter with relevant prior study), on campus (Melbourne or Sydney)
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree in any discipline
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

Advanced Diploma of Jewellery and Object Design

Bachelor of Accounting
description:
When Melbourne Polytechnic launched this course it was the first of its kind in Victoria - an accounting degree built explicitly around sustainable business rather than treating environmental and social accounting as an afterthought elective. Alongside the expected run of taxation, auditing and corporate accounting units, students take environmental law, economics and policy subjects that most accounting degrees skip entirely.

It's dual-accredited with CPA Australia and Chartered Accountants Australia & New Zealand, so graduates are eligible for associate CPA membership straight out of the degree - a genuine professional pathway, not marketing language. Students can also add a Business Analytics major or a Marketing specialisation on top of the core accounting sequence, which is unusual flexibility for what's fundamentally a professional accreditation degree; most accounting programs elsewhere lock students into a rigid sequence with no room to move.

Career outcomes span the expected accountant/auditor/tax consultant roles but also lean toward sustainability-adjacent finance work - ESG reporting, environmental compliance auditing - reflecting the degree's original design brief.
curriculum:
Year 1: Financial Accounting, Business Law, Microeconomics, Quantitative Methods for Business, Business Communication
Year 2: Management Accounting, Corporate Accounting, Taxation Law, Auditing Principles, Environmental Law and Policy
Year 3: Advanced Taxation, Financial Statement Analysis, Sustainability Accounting, capstone accounting project, plus Business Analytics or Marketing specialisation electives
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; VET pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Agriculture and Technology (Agronomy)
description:
Agronomy at Melbourne Polytechnic focuses on crop and pasture management with sustainability and production efficiency as the throughline - how to get a paddock producing well without running the soil down over a decade. It shares the same first-year foundation as the college's other agriculture majors, so students arrive at the agronomy specialisation with a grounding in plant and soil science rather than jumping straight into crop-specific technical content.

Because Melbourne Polytechnic teaches agriculture with a metropolitan base but rural training sites, agronomy students get exposure to broadacre cropping and pasture systems without needing to relocate for the full three years - useful for students balancing farm work or family commitments back home with formal study. The degree leans toward the technical and advisory side of agronomy rather than pure research, preparing graduates for consulting and agribusiness roles rather than academic pathways.

Typical outcomes include agronomist, agricultural consultant, farm advisory roles and positions with agribusiness input suppliers - the kind of jobs where a farmer calls you about a crop problem and expects a diagnosis, not a literature review.
curriculum:
Year 1 (shared foundation): Plant Science Fundamentals, Soil Science, Farm Business Management, Sustainable Land Management
Year 2: Crop Production Systems, Pasture Management, Plant Nutrition, Weed and Pest Management
Year 3: Precision Agriculture, Agribusiness and Advisory Practice, industry placement with an agronomy consultancy or agribusiness, capstone project
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; VET pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Agriculture and Technology (Horticulture)
description:
The horticulture major sits inside Melbourne Polytechnic's broader Agriculture and Technology degree, sharing first-year foundation subjects with the viticulture, agronomy and sports turf majors before students specialise. That shared first year means students who aren't sure whether they want production horticulture, amenity horticulture or something closer to agronomy get a genuine look at all of it before committing.

Teaching draws on the same land-based facilities the college uses across its agriculture programs - working farms and growing areas rather than purely classroom instruction - and the emphasis stays practical throughout: plant identification, propagation, irrigation and pest management taught as things you do, not just things you're tested on. Career paths span nursery management, landscape horticulture, parks and gardens roles, and technical horticulture positions with wholesale growers.

Three years full-time, with the same part-time and mixed-mode flexibility offered across the Agriculture and Technology suite for students juggling work or living outside Melbourne.
curriculum:
Year 1 (shared with other Agriculture and Technology majors): Plant Science Fundamentals, Soil Science, Farm Business Management, Sustainable Land Management
Year 2: Plant Propagation and Nursery Production, Irrigation Systems, Pest and Disease Management, Landscape Design Principles
Year 3: Advanced Horticultural Production, Amenity Horticulture Management, industry placement, capstone research project
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; VET pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Agriculture and Technology (Sports Turf Science and Management)
description:
This is the one nobody else in Australia offers at higher-education level - Melbourne Polytechnic runs the only bachelor's-level Sports Turf Science and Management course in the country, backed by the Australian Sports Turf Managers Association (ASTMA). That's not a minor claim; anyone wanting to move beyond a turf-management certificate into a genuine degree in this field has essentially one option, and this is it.

The course covers turf agronomy, drainage and irrigation engineering, and sports surface management across the range of playing surfaces - ovals, greens, pitches - that professional and community sporting facilities actually run on. Career paths go well beyond "head groundskeeper": turf consulting, research and development, and commercial roles with turf equipment and chemical suppliers all draw from this graduate pool, and the ASTMA connection means students get exposure to industry conferences and networks most turf programs don't offer.

Shares the same first-year agriculture foundation as the college's viticulture, horticulture and agronomy majors before specialising from second year.
curriculum:
Year 1 (shared foundation): Plant Science Fundamentals, Soil Science, Farm Business Management, Sustainable Land Management
Year 2: Turf Grass Science, Sports Surface Construction and Drainage, Irrigation Design for Turf, Turf Pest and Disease Management
Year 3: Sports Turf Facility Management, Turf Equipment and Machinery Systems, industry placement at a sporting venue or turf consultancy, capstone project
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; VET pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Agriculture and Technology (Viticulture and Winemaking)
description:
Melbourne Polytechnic is the only metropolitan provider in Victoria running this course, and it teaches on working wineries rather than simulated ones - a 100-tonne winery at Epping and a 250-tonne winery at the Ararat Training Centre, plus more than 40 hectares of vineyards spread across Ararat, the Yarra Valley and the Northern Lodge Training Centre at Eden Park. Vintage work happens on real fruit that becomes real bottled wine, not a classroom exercise that gets tipped down a drain.

Three years full-time (part-time available), delivered as a mix of face-to-face and online so students who work full-time or live outside Melbourne aren't locked out. The degree covers both ends of the trade - vineyard management and winemaking chemistry - so graduates aren't pigeonholed into one half of the industry. Career outcomes run from vineyard manager and viticulturist through to winemaker, agronomist and rural business manager, with the Ararat facility in particular giving students exposure to a cooler-climate growing region distinct from what they'd see purely around Melbourne.
curriculum:
Year 1: Introduction to Viticulture, Plant and Soil Science, Wine Chemistry Fundamentals, Farm Business Management
Year 2: Vineyard Establishment and Management, Winemaking Practice I, Pest and Disease Management, Sensory Evaluation
Year 3: Winemaking Practice II (vintage placement), Wine Business and Marketing, Sustainable Viticulture, capstone research project
Vintage placements at the Epping and Ararat wineries run across both winemaking practice units
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; VET pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Applied Architecture
description:
Melbourne Polytechnic runs credit points the way most Victorian TAFEs do - 12 credit points per subject, 96 per full-time year - and the Applied Architecture degree uses that structure to move students through architectural software, design studio work and sustainability principles at a pace that assumes no prior design background. It's aimed at people who want to work in architectural practice as designers and documenters, not necessarily become registered architects through the traditional five-year-plus pathway.

Studio culture here is smaller and more hands-on than what you'd get at a large university architecture school - critiques happen in rooms of a dozen or so rather than lecture halls of 200, and staff are often practising architects or building designers rather than purely academic researchers. The course threads environmental sustainability principles and responses to natural and built environments through the design studios rather than treating sustainability as a bolt-on unit.

Graduates commonly move into architectural technologist, building designer and documentation roles within practices, or continue into further architecture study if registration is the eventual goal.
curriculum:
Year 1: Design Studio 1 and 2, Architectural Communication, Building Construction Fundamentals, History and Theory of Architecture
Year 2: Design Studio 3 and 4, Structures for Architecture, Environmentally Sustainable Design, Digital Documentation (BIM/CAD)
Year 3: Design Studio 5 and 6, Professional Practice, capstone design project, industry-linked studio brief
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; VET pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Business
description:
First-year Bachelor of Business students at Melbourne Polytechnic all sit the same foundation subjects - accounting basics, economics, marketing principles, business communication - before picking a direction. From second year they specialise into one of three streams: Management, Marketing or Entrepreneurship, choosing electives that build toward whichever one fits.

The entrepreneurship stream is the one that gets talked about most, partly because Melbourne Polytechnic runs it with actual startup mentoring and pitch events rather than just a unit called "Entrepreneurship 101." Students in that stream often leave with something they've actually built or tested, not just a business plan sitting in a folder. The management and marketing streams are more conventional but still keep a practical, small-business bent that suits the kind of student who wants to run something rather than analyse a multinational from a distance.

Because it sits within a dual-sector institution, students who aren't sure business is for them can often move sideways into a related diploma without losing credit, and those coming up from Melbourne Polytechnic's own diplomas can usually get credit going the other way. Three years full-time, campus-based teaching at Preston or the CBD campus depending on intake.
curriculum:
Year 1: Introduction to Management, Accounting for Business, Marketing Principles, Business Economics, Business Communication, Business Law
Year 2: choice of stream - Management (Organisational Behaviour, Human Resource Management), Marketing (Consumer Behaviour, Digital Marketing) or Entrepreneurship (New Venture Creation, Innovation Management) - plus core Business Statistics and Business Ethics
Year 3: Strategic Management, work-integrated learning placement, capstone business project, stream electives
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; VET pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Education (Early Years and Primary)
Bachelor of Engineering Technology (Civil)
description:
This is a four-year degree, longer than the typical three-year applied bachelor's, and the extra year buys something real: everyone does the same core civil engineering subjects for the first two years, then in years three and four splits into structural engineering, municipal/transportation, or construction management. Nobody has to decide their specialty at eighteen before they've poured a single test cylinder of concrete.

Work-integrated learning is threaded through the degree rather than bolted on as a single placement block at the end - students work alongside industry partners on real projects, which matters in civil engineering more than most fields because so much of the job is site-specific judgment that a lecture theatre can't teach. Entry requires a selection interview on top of academic results, which filters for people who actually want to build roads and drainage systems rather than just wanting an engineering degree in the abstract.

Graduates land in urban planning, infrastructure delivery, geotechnical consulting and site engineering roles, largely across Melbourne's outer-suburban growth corridors where Melbourne Polytechnic's Preston and Epping campuses are well placed.
curriculum:
Years 1-2 (core, shared): Engineering Mathematics, Mechanics of Materials, Surveying, Construction Materials, Hydraulics, Geotechnical Engineering, CAD and Engineering Drawing, Project Management Fundamentals
Associate Degree exit point available after year 2
Years 3-4: choice of stream - Structural Engineering (Structural Analysis and Design, Advanced Structures), Municipal/Transportation (Road Design, Water and Wastewater Systems), or Construction Management (Contract Administration, Construction Planning)
Final year: Work Integrated Learning placement with an industry partner, capstone engineering project
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion with mathematics; VET pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

name: Bachelor of Information Technology
description:
The Bachelor of IT here runs on 24 subjects total - 14 core, 6 in a chosen major, 4 electives - and that structure matters because it means students commit to a specialisation (Software Development, Network Development or Business Analytics) without locking themselves out of everything else; electives can be pulled from whichever of the other majors interests them, or from other higher-education courses on offer, by arrangement with the head of discipline.

It's ACS-accredited, which for a lot of applicants is the whole point - it satisfies the skills-assessment pathway that migration agents ask about constantly. Melbourne Polytechnic also has the SAS Institute partnership feeding into the Business Analytics major, so students there can walk out with a SAS Academic Specialisation alongside the degree itself, which is a genuine differentiator against similar bachelor's programs at bigger universities that don't have that industry tie-up.

Students who want to leave early - a change of plan, a job offer, a visa issue - can exit after 16 subjects with an Associate Degree, which is a safety net most three-year IT degrees don't build in explicitly.
curriculum:
Year 1: Programming Fundamentals, Database Design, Web Development, Networking Essentials, IT Project Fundamentals, Systems Analysis
Year 2: major begins - Software Development / Network Development / Business Analytics core units - plus Operating Systems, Data Structures and Algorithms
Year 3: advanced major units, 4 electives (drawn from other majors or negotiated), industry capstone project
Exit point after 16 subjects: Associate Degree in Information Technology
admission_requirements: Year 12 completion or equivalent; VET pathway available
english_requirements: IELTS 6.0 (no band below 6.0) or equivalent

description:
Melbourne Polytechnic's Master of IT is built for people who already have a degree in something else and want a fast, credible route into tech. Most cohorts are a mix of career-changers - former accountants, engineers, nurses - and international students chasing an ICT-eligible qualification, and the teaching reflects that: less theory-for-its-own-sake, more "here's how a helpdesk escalation actually gets triaged" or "here's what a real data pipeline looks like when the source data is a mess."

Students choose a major in either Cyber Security or Data Analytics partway through. The cyber stream leans on Melbourne Polytechnic's security labs and covers penetration testing, incident response and governance frameworks rather than just theory; the data analytics stream uses SAS software under the college's long-running partnership with SAS Institute, so graduates finish with an industry credential most competitors don't hand out. Class sizes in the specialist units are small enough that lecturers know who's struggling with SQL joins by week three.

It's a two-year full-time course (part-time options exist for people working while they study), and because it's TAFE-adjacent rather than a sandstone university, fees sit well below comparable Melbourne master's programs while still carrying full postgraduate status for visa and PR-pathway purposes.
curriculum:
Year 1, Semester 1: Programming Principles, Database Systems, IT Project Management, Systems Analysis and Design
Year 1, Semester 2: Network Fundamentals, Advanced Programming, Cyber Security Fundamentals, Cloud Computing
Year 2, Semester 1: Major stream begins - Cyber Security (Penetration Testing, Security Governance and Risk) or Data Analytics (SAS Programming, Predictive Modelling)
Year 2, Semester 2: Capstone Industry Project, Emerging Technologies, elective from the alternate major
Assessment mix: applied labs, client-based capstone project, case study reports rather than closed-book exams in most units
admission_requirements: Bachelor's degree (any discipline) typically required (approximate, typical bar, not program-page-verified)
english_requirements: IELTS 6.5 overall (typical bar, approximate)

Because accounting requires professional judgement as much as technical calculation, the course also builds ethical reasoning and governance principles into the curriculum, reflecting the profession's role in verifying and reporting on an organisation's financial position. The degree blends conceptual theory with practical application throughout, rather than saving real-world context for later years, so graduates leave with both the technical grounding needed for professional accreditation and the analytical skills to interpret what the numbers actually mean for a business. It suits students who know from the outset that they want a career in accounting, audit or financial analysis, whether in public practice, corporate finance teams or government, and the degree's structure supports progression into CA ANZ or CPA Australia membership pathways after graduation.

name: Bachelor of Actuarial Science
description: Monash's Bachelor of Actuarial Science trains students for the long, technically demanding path toward becoming a qualified actuary, starting with foundational mathematics and statistics before moving into applied actuarial modelling. Two specialisation streams, actuarial studies and actuarial analytics, let students shape the degree toward traditional actuarial practice or a more data-and-analytics-heavy career, and the course builds in opportunities for industry-based experience so students graduate with more than classroom exposure to the field. Because full actuarial accreditation in Australia requires professional exams and several years of supervised experience after university, the degree is best understood as the first, most technically rigorous stage of a longer qualification process rather than a complete professional credential on its own. Career paths span life, general and health insurance, superannuation, risk management and financial consulting, and many graduates move into investment operations at asset managers, brokers or banks, while others take government roles in regulatory or workers' compensation settings.

name: Bachelor of Aerospace Engineering (Honours)
description: Monash's Bachelor of Aerospace Engineering (Honours) starts with a common first-year engineering program shared across all engineering branches, giving students hands-on design-and-build experience before they commit to aerospace as their specific specialisation from second year onward. Once specialised, students build in-depth technical knowledge of aerospace-specific engineering methods, tools and design techniques, alongside the project management skills needed to run engineering projects rather than just contribute technical work to them. High-achieving students can fast-track into the Master of Engineering through an accelerated pathway, using electives during the bachelor's degree to complete master's-level units and graduating with both an honours bachelor's degree and an expert master's degree in a fraction of the usual combined time. It suits students committed to an aerospace engineering career from early in their studies, and the shared first year gives some flexibility to switch into a different engineering specialisation if aerospace turns out not to be the right fit after initial exposure.

name: Bachelor of Agentic Software Engineering
description: Monash's Bachelor of Agentic Software Engineering is a new degree focused specifically on building software systems with AI components, agentic workflows and human-AI collaboration, rather than treating AI as a specialisation within a general software engineering degree. Students build a strong software engineering foundation alongside training in judgement, quality, security, usability and responsible AI practices across the full software development lifecycle, reflecting how much software engineering work now involves integrating AI components rather than writing conventional code alone. Embedded professional practice units and work-integrated learning opportunities run throughout the degree, so students graduate with a portfolio demonstrating real technical capability rather than only academic results. It suits students who want to work specifically at the intersection of software engineering and applied AI, positioning graduates for roles building AI-powered products and systems as agentic software becomes standard across the tech industry. Entry requires an ATAR of around 80 at Clayton, along with Units 3-4 English and Mathematical Methods or Specialist Mathematics.
admission_requirements: ATAR 80 (Clayton). Requires English (Units 3-4, study score 25+) and, for most of these courses, Mathematical Methods or Specialist Mathematics (study score 22-25+). VET and higher-education pathway entry also available.

name: Bachelor of Applied Data Science

Students choose a stream to apply their data science skills toward, whether that's physical sciences, sociology and anthropology, business or engineering, meaning the degree can lead toward quite different career directions depending on which stream a student picks. That combination of technical data skills and a chosen application domain is designed to make graduates genuinely versatile problem solvers across industries that increasingly rely on data-driven decision-making, from policy and NGOs to corporate strategy and scientific research. It suits students who want the technical rigor of a data science degree without being confined to a single industry application, keeping career options open across the public, private and non-profit sectors.

description: Monash's Bachelor of International Relations examines power, governance, conflict and cooperation at local, national and global levels, teaching students how political institutions actually operate and why conflict and cooperation occur between states and other political actors. On graduation, students gain provisional registration with Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia, moving into a compulsory hospital internship year before full registration and further specialty training in fields like general practice, surgery or psychiatry.

Clinical placements span metropolitan and rural health services, with increasing complexity through third and fourth year, and students spend time working alongside other health science students including occupational therapy, nursing and nutrition and dietetics to build interprofessional collaboration skills. The course exposes students to the specialty areas physiotherapists commonly work in, including cardiorespiratory care, gerontology, neurological rehabilitation and musculoskeletal or sports physiotherapy, without requiring specialisation before graduation. On completion, graduates are eligible for registration with the Physiotherapy Board of Australia, which covers practice rights across every state and territory. Physiotherapists trained through this degree go on to work in public and private hospitals, sports medicine clinics, rehabilitation centres, aged care and private practice, as well as in health promotion, management and research roles.

description: Monash College's Diploma of Science is a pathway into second year of a Monash University Science degree, introducing the fundamentals of the scientific method in both theory and practice across chemistry, physics, biology, mathematics, psychology, computing and engineering-related units. Part 1 builds core science subjects across these disciplines, while Part 2 has students studying the same subjects as first-year Monash University students, developing specialist knowledge in whichever science area they intend to major in later. Assessment includes group projects, oral and poster presentations and a final exam, reflecting both the collaborative and individually assessed sides of university science study. International students who complete Part 2 gain direct entry into second year of their Monash Science degree, while domestic students can enter first year after Part 1 or second year after Part 2. It suits students aiming for a science career at Monash who need an alternative entry route due to academic score, English proficiency or an international qualification gap.

Because the specific research topic and discipline depend entirely on the individual student's area of interest within the sciences, spanning anything from chemistry to physics to environmental science, the actual content of any given PhD varies enormously between candidates. Graduates demonstrate they've designed and executed a research project making an original and substantial contribution to their field, alongside developing the professional skills needed to make an impact across academia, industry, government or community settings. It suits science graduates with a strong existing research background, typically an honours degree or research master's, who have identified a specific research question they want to pursue over several years of doctoral study.

description: The Doctor of Physiotherapy is Monash's graduate-entry route into physiotherapy practice, designed for students who already hold an undergraduate science degree and want a fast, focused path to registration rather than starting a four-year undergraduate program. Delivered at the Peninsula campus over three years, the course builds an integrated curriculum across musculoskeletal, neurological and cardiorespiratory physiotherapy, combining case-based learning with early clinical placements that expand into acute, subacute and community settings by the second and third year. A final-year selective placement and independent research project let students shape the degree toward the area of practice they're most drawn to, whether that's sports physiotherapy, aged care or rehabilitation. Graduates meet Physiotherapy Board of Australia registration requirements and the course aligns with practice thresholds recognised in both Australia and New Zealand, so it opens the door to physiotherapy careers on either side of the Tasman as well as further international registration in many countries.

Graduates meet Podiatry Board of Australia registration requirements, including endorsement to use scheduled medicines, which matters because it lets Monash-trained podiatrists prescribe certain medications independently rather than always referring out. It suits science graduates who've decided on podiatry as a healthcare career, offering a faster, more focused path to registration than restarting an undergraduate podiatry degree, and the accelerated three-year structure assumes students arrive with a solid foundational science background already in place.

You pick your four units from the wide pool taught across Monash Business School's coursework master's degrees, so the certificate can lean toward marketing, human resources, public sector management, economics or a health economics stream run through the Centre for Health Economics. Because the units are drawn straight from the master's curriculum, the credit typically carries forward if you decide to continue into a Graduate Diploma of Business or a specialist master's later. The course suits people with a non-business first degree who need a fast, credible way to pick up core commercial concepts, or professionals using their work experience in place of a bachelor's degree for entry. name: Master of Advanced Study (Engineering Research)
description: Monash's Master of Advanced Study (Engineering Research) is a research-only degree in which students independently investigate a research problem in engineering that they formulate themselves, working under a dedicated supervisory team rather than following set coursework units. Because there's no fixed curriculum, the actual content and direction of study depends entirely on the individual research topic and the student's chosen engineering discipline, making the course fundamentally different from a coursework master's degree. It suits engineering graduates who already have a genuine research question they want to pursue and are looking for a credential that reflects independent research capability, often as a pathway toward a PhD or a research career in industry or academia. Entry requires strong prior academic performance, typically an honours degree with an upper second-class result or completion of Part 1 of the same master's program, reflecting the research-intensive nature of the degree. It suits biomedical science graduates who have a genuine research question they want to pursue and are considering further research study or a research career, rather than students wanting a taught postgraduate qualification with a fixed curriculum.

It suits science graduates who want to combine technical biotechnology depth with genuine commercial and entrepreneurial skills, positioning them for roles that bridge research and industry rather than staying purely in the lab.

Depending on prior study you complete 72 or 96 credit points, and within that you can either keep your unit choices spread across disciplines or commit to one of several named specialisations including business economics, entrepreneurship, financial and risk management, international business, marketing, project management, and supply chain management. The course pitches itself around professional development and social responsibility as much as technical business skills, aiming to produce graduates who can operate in complex organisations while being conscious of governance and sustainability constraints. Entry requires a bachelor's degree in any discipline with at least a credit average, making it one of the more accessible routes into Monash's postgraduate business school for non-business graduates.

Online delivery lets students start within weeks of applying and fit study around existing work and family commitments, reflecting the degree's design for working professionals rather than full-time students. Depending on prior qualifications, students complete either 72 or 48 credit points, with graduates of Monash's Graduate Certificate of Business Administration entering at the shorter pathway. It suits experienced professionals moving into or already working in strategic management and leadership roles who need an MBA that treats ongoing digital and technological change as central content rather than an add-on module, and entry requires a bachelor's degree with a credit average plus three years of relevant professional experience.

name: Master of Clinical Embryology
description: Monash's Master of Clinical Embryology is a 12-month, laboratory-focused course built specifically to prepare graduates for entry-level roles in IVF clinics, covering the practical, ethical and regulatory sides of human infertility treatment. Students spend the year on continual practical skills training using mouse and ovine IVF as laboratory models, since the course involves no direct patient contact, alongside a minor research project and coursework covering the national and international regulations that govern human IVF services. A mid-year placement at an Australian, New Zealand or international IVF clinic gives students direct exposure to clinical operations before graduation. Because the course is recognised across most Australian IVF clinics, graduates are often placed directly into entry-level embryology positions, with a realistic path to lab manager roles later in their career. Online delivery is available, with practical experience gained largely in the student's own workplace supplemented by occasional on-campus workshops, making the course accessible to people already working adjacent to the fertility sector.

A supervised clinical research project with scope for real community impact runs alongside the clinical training, reflecting the course's stated commitment to research-informed clinical practice rather than purely applied skills training. It suits psychology honours or equivalent graduates aiming specifically for registration as a clinical psychologist, as opposed to general registration through the Master of Professional Psychology, and the emphasis on cultural responsiveness and complex mental health presentations prepares graduates for varied community and clinical settings.

Students choose between a clinical research specialisation, covering biostatistics, epidemiology, clinical trials and systematic review methods, or a translational research specialisation focused on how research findings in areas like central nervous system disorders, metabolic disease and immunology move from the lab into clinical application. Both pathways include a substantial supervised research project that lets students develop their own research question within their chosen specialisation, taught by clinical and research academics working at a major teaching hospital. name: Master of Commerce
description: The Master of Commerce functions as pre-doctoral training at Monash rather than a standalone professional degree, built for high-achieving students who intend to go on to a Monash PhD in a business or economics discipline. Across the course you complete advanced coursework alongside supervised research methodology training, then design and carry out independent research in your chosen specialisation under close supervision, effectively rehearsing the doctoral process before committing to it. It's the compulsory pathway into PhD study for banking and finance, and the preferred pathway for accounting, econometrics and business statistics, economics, health economics, management and marketing studies specialisations. Entry is competitive, generally requiring a distinction average in relevant third-year units on top of a bachelor's degree in a related discipline. This isn't the right course for someone seeking a terminal master's qualification for industry; it exists specifically to prepare strong students for doctoral research and Monash assesses progression into the PhD on the same selection standards used for direct PhD entry.

name: Master of Counselling
description: Monash's Master of Counselling builds a professional counselling qualification through applied and experiential learning rather than a primarily theoretical approach, taught by staff who bring their own experience as practising counsellors or psychologists into how they teach the material. Students develop expertise working with individuals, couples, families and groups, learning contemporary evidence-based counselling approaches for assessment and intervention across diverse populations, and refine their own counselling style through supervised professional placements. The structure assumes students want to graduate ready to practise, so assessment leans heavily on applying theory to real counselling scenarios rather than testing theoretical recall alone. It suits people planning a career as a professional counsellor across mental health, community, education or workplace settings, and offers more depth and a fuller professional qualification than Monash's shorter Graduate Certificate of Counselling for students who know counselling is their long-term career direction.

name: Master of Cultural and Creative Industries
description: Monash's Master of Cultural and Creative Industries examines the trends and challenges facing creative practitioners, cultural managers, entrepreneurs and policymakers, drawing on Monash academics across cultural management, cultural policy, film and media studies, and cultural economics. Being based in Melbourne, Australia's cultural hub, gives the course access to genuine industry internships and field trips rather than studying the creative sector purely from the classroom. Graduates have gone on to roles including business development manager, public relations manager, social media content creator, events project manager, arts administrator and community engagement officer, reflecting the genuinely broad range of careers the cultural and creative sector actually offers. It suits graduates with an arts, media, communications or business background who want to move specifically into cultural sector management or creative industry leadership roles, rather than a purely academic qualification in cultural studies.

name: Master of Cybersecurity
description: Monash's Master of Cybersecurity trains students to manage and administer both cybersecurity and blockchain systems, preparing graduates for roles including security systems analyst, systems designer, data communications specialist and security software engineer or administrator. The course sits within Monash's Faculty of IT, giving students access to genuine technical infrastructure and expertise rather than a business-school treatment of cybersecurity as a governance and compliance topic alone. It suits computing, IT or engineering graduates who want to specialise specifically in the technical and operational side of cybersecurity, positioning them for roles defending organisational systems and data against an increasingly sophisticated range of digital threats. The blockchain component reflects growing demand for security expertise that extends beyond traditional network defence into the newer technical domains organisations are now trying to secure.

name: Master of Data Science
description: Monash's Master of Data Science builds skills across data analysis, data engineering and big data processing, covering statistical machine learning, exploratory analysis and working with structured and semi-structured data sets, while also examining how data science actually affects organisations and society rather than treating it as a purely technical discipline. Notably, entry doesn't require an IT background: students can enter with any bachelor's degree at a credit average, though those without a cognate IT, business, engineering or science background with programming and mathematics experience take the longer, two-year entry pathway rather than the accelerated 18-month option. Students finish with either a research project or a team-based industry experience studio project, letting them choose between an academic and a more applied capstone experience. It suits graduates from any discipline who've decided data science is their next career step, as well as those with an existing quantitative or IT background wanting the faster pathway into data science specialisation.

name: Master of Design (by Research)
description: Monash's Master of Design (by Research) is a studio-based research degree where students develop an original body of design work, spanning graphic design, industrial design, interior architecture or multimedia, accompanied by written and visual documentation that provides critical context for the work rather than treating design purely as a practical skill. Unlike a coursework design master's, students must produce genuinely new work created during their enrolment, since design completed before or outside the degree can't be included in the final exhibition and assessment. Entry requires strong prior academic performance, typically an honours degree with an upper second-class result or equivalent, and applicants must demonstrate real capacity for independent research. It suits design graduates who want to pursue an original, self-directed design research project at a genuinely advanced level, rather than students looking for taught coursework in a specific design discipline.

name: Master of Dietetics
description: The Master of Nutrition and Dietetics at Monash University develops the professional and personal qualities required for practice as an accredited dietitian across a variety of workplaces. The coursework degree provides knowledge and skills across clinical dietetics, food service, and community and public health nutrition, with professional practice placements, and offers a clear pathway for PhD entry. Graduates are eligible for accreditation as practising dietitians.

name: Master of Economics
description: Monash's Master of Economics builds advanced theoretical understanding of economics alongside its practical application to government and business decision-making, aimed at early-career economists and recent graduates who want to deepen their expertise in applied economic analysis and independent research. Students can develop deep knowledge in development economics or policy economics, or build a custom stream by selecting units that match their specific career goals, covering areas like competition policy, project evaluation, pricing, risk and regulation. The course blends conceptual theory with practical application from the start rather than saving real-world context for later units, reflecting its target audience of students who already have some economics background and want to extend it rather than start from scratch. It suits graduates aiming for economist roles in government, the corporate sector or research institutions, particularly those wanting exposure to the global economy and international economic policy questions.

name: Master of Education
description: Monash's Master of Education lets educators from early childhood, schools, higher education, workplace training and community settings choose a specialisation that matches their actual career context rather than following one generic education curriculum. Available specialisations include early childhood education, digital learning, inclusive and special education and general education studies, with mathematics leadership, STEM education and social justice specialisations offered on a more limited, cohort basis in some years. Flexible full-time or part-time study and a range of flexibly taught units accommodate working educators, and strong students can extend into a higher degree by research if they want to keep building toward doctoral study. It's important to note this course does not provide an initial teaching qualification. It's built for people who are already educators, or working in education-adjacent roles, who want to deepen expertise in a specific area rather than qualify to teach for the first time.

description: Monash's Master of Educational and Developmental Psychology is accredited by the Australian Psychology Accreditation Council as the fifth and sixth year of psychology training, preparing graduates to practise as educational and developmental psychologists across schools, health services, hospitals, clinics and corporate settings. The course builds evidence-based practice skills in assessment, therapy and applied research, aiming to produce independent professionals who can think critically about the psychological processes involved in learning and development across the lifespan rather than only in childhood. Because it covers two full accreditation levels in one course, it suits psychology graduates who are confident about specialising in educational and developmental psychology specifically, as distinct from clinical or professional psychology's broader scope. Graduates go on to work directly with children, families and schools, as well as in broader developmental psychology roles across health and community services.

A pathway into a higher degree by research is available for graduates who want to keep building academic expertise in educational leadership after finishing the master's, making the course a viable stepping stone toward doctoral study as well as a standalone leadership qualification.

name: Master of Engineering
description: Monash's Master of Engineering extends an existing engineering undergraduate degree into a chosen specialisation, covering engineering management, biological, civil, electrical, energy transitions, materials, mechanical, power systems, renewable energy and smart manufacturing engineering. Rather than repeating undergraduate content, the course builds leadership and complex problem-solving skills in a genuinely cross-cultural environment, assuming students already have the technical grounding from their first engineering degree. It suits engineering graduates who want deeper technical specialisation or a leadership-oriented extension to their qualification without duplicating undergraduate coursework, and it's shorter than starting a second bachelor's degree in a different engineering discipline. The wide range of specialisations means the course can serve very different career directions, from a mechanical engineer moving into renewable energy to a civil engineer specialising in materials, depending entirely on which specialisation a student selects.

name: Master of Engineering Science (Research)
description: Monash's Master of Engineering Science (Research) is a research-only degree where students independently investigate a self-formulated engineering research problem under supervision, rather than completing a fixed set of coursework units. Because the course structure is entirely research-driven, the specific content and direction depends on the individual student's chosen engineering discipline and research question, making it fundamentally different from any of Monash's coursework engineering master's degrees. It suits engineering graduates who already have a genuine research question they want to pursue and are considering further research study or a research-focused engineering career, often as a pathway toward doctoral study, rather than students seeking a taught engineering specialisation with a set curriculum. Applicants need to demonstrate real capacity for independent research and adequate prior training.

name: Master of Environment and Sustainability
description: Monash's Master of Environment and Sustainability is a two-year interdisciplinary course that connects global change knowledge with sustainability principles, built around the understanding that social, economic and environmental systems are deeply interdependent rather than separable problems. name: Master of Transport and Mobility Planning
description: Monash's Master of Transport and Mobility Planning tackles the interrelated social, economic and environmental factors driving transport policy, infrastructure and land use decisions in modern cities, combining theoretical coursework with project-based real-world case studies. The course covers multi-modal traffic engineering and management, travel demand modelling, and the economic factors that shape transport infrastructure decisions, alongside a dedicated research methods component that builds the analytical skills needed to evaluate transportation projects rigorously. A strong emphasis on integrating new technology into urban planning reflects how much transport planning has changed with the arrival of ride-sharing, electric vehicles and changing commuting patterns since the pandemic. It suits graduates from planning, engineering, geography or related backgrounds aiming for careers as transportation planners, urban mobility consultants or policy analysts in government or the private sector, particularly those interested in the technology and sustainability dimensions of how cities move people and goods.

name: Bachelor of Applied Social Care
description:
A three-year degree in applied social care, developed with industry and community partners for roles across the care and community services sector. Students choose one major from Child and Family Studies, Human Behaviour, International Aid and Development, Sociology, or Foundations of Business Management, and build practical skills through internships and placements with community organisations, government agencies and not-for-profits.

Students who want that should look at an accredited Bachelor of Social Work. Entry is an ATAR of about 70, with Murdoch RISE adjustments and other alternative pathways available. Graduates work as child, family and youth support workers, disability support workers, care coordinators and community services officers. Graduates work as policy and project officers, communications and media advisers, researchers and community development workers across government, international development, media and the not-for-profit sector. name: Bachelor of Business
description:
Murdoch's Bachelor of Business runs on a major-first model. The degree itself is broad, and the substance comes from choosing among majors including Accounting, Banking, Business Law, Entrepreneurship and Innovation, Finance, Hospitality and Tourism Management, Human Resources Management (with AHRI accreditation available), Management, and Marketing. Because majors are tied to the degree rather than offered as standalone qualifications, students effectively pick their specialisation after enrolling rather than applying into it directly.

An elective Work Integrated Learning program is the degree's most concrete differentiator: students take on real projects and internships with organisations that have included local government bodies, Myer, and RAC Arena, giving business students the kind of client-facing experience that's usually reserved for professional-track degrees like law or engineering. It's optional rather than compulsory, so outcomes vary a lot depending on whether a given student opts in.

The core skill set the university emphasises (critical thinking, financial literacy, data-informed decision-making, ethics) reads as fairly standard business-school language, but the WIL placements are where the degree's actual differentiation from a generic business degree shows up in practice.

Year 1: business core (accounting principles, economics, business law, marketing fundamentals, quantitative methods for business)
Year 2: major sequence begins (choice of Accounting, Banking, Business Law, Entrepreneurship and Innovation, Finance, Hospitality and Tourism Management, HR Management, Management, or Marketing), business analytics
Year 3: advanced major units, elective Work Integrated Learning placement (internship or industry project), capstone business strategy unit
Total: 3 years full-time; WIL placements available with employers including local government, retail and major venues
